debate_title: As AI automates cognitive labor, should policy prioritize...

conflicts.point: Whether handing a worker open model weights transfers the surplus, or whether the high-skill integration labor (fine-tuning, evaluation, production operations) and the compute to run at scale mean the value still accrues to compute owners.

positions.stance: A worker running an open model captures the productivity delta and becomes the deployer; the residual barrier is a training-access gap closable by funding public capacity and reforming fair use, not a structural impossibility.

Open weights distribute risk to the individual but not the delta; the same deskilling trajectory denies workers the mastery to deploy, so surplus flows to whoever owns the compute, reproducing the Engels Pause gap.

conflicts.point: Whether an independent-reporting-line body can effectively audit where AI surplus is booked and redirect it.

positions.stance: A body with independent reporting lines, a statutory mandate to audit booked-value capture, and authority to halt the flow of surplus is a viable architecture distinct from the captured referee.

The IRS, the best-funded booked-value auditor, loses roughly $160 billion a year to transfer-pricing and IP-migration games, so an independent reporting line for AI surplus is a whiteboard sketch until a working deployment is shown.

conflicts.point: What 'worker ownership' must mean to capture surplus — access to the tool, an audited transfer decided on the worker's behalf, or a contractual bargaining mechanism with the power to refuse.

positions.stance: Real ownership is a bargaining mechanism — the power to refuse, organize, or claim a written share of surplus; neither distribution-by-access nor surplus-by-audit puts a worker at the table.
Owning the tool (open weights plus funded access) is the institutional claim, letting the worker capture the delta directly without a referee deciding on their behalf.
A named actor auditing booked value and able to redirect surplus is the enforceable claim; access alone leaves the worker with the burden and the surplus offshore.

conflicts.point: Whether current AI adoption in clerical and support work is regenerative dynamism that creates new roles or pure labor-arbitrage substitution.

positions.stance: Most current adoption swaps a $25/hour task for a $2 inference call — substitution wearing a dynamism costume; measured deployments like GitHub Copilot raise output while wages stay flat.

Conceded that most current adoption is cost-cutting arbitrage, but maintains faster displacement is the argument for faster transition tooling and that net cognitive-labor demand has not gone permanently to zero in any sector.

verdicts.conflict: Whether handing a worker open model weights transfers the productivity surplus, or whether integration labor and compute ownership mean value still accrues to compute owners.
verdicts.rationale: The position that surplus flows to compute owners cites a concrete deployment (GitHub Copilot raising developer output while wages stay flat) showing operating a tool does not capture the delta, plus a specific infrastructure constraint (IEA projecting AI data-center electricity demand to quadruple by 2030 with production-scale compute concentrated in a handful of sites). The access-transfers-surplus position rests on a deductive argument (a weights file cannot be relocated like payroll) but concedes the compute layer is unsolved (C22), which undercuts its claim that the surplus question is answered. The Copilot counterexample directly addresses the mechanism in dispute and is not rebutted with comparable evidence.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: A documented case of workers holding open weights capturing the productivity delta as income—rather than ceding it to employers or compute providers—after public capacity funding and fair-use reform, would shift the balance toward the access position.

verdicts.conflict: Whether an independent-reporting-line body can effectively audit where AI surplus is booked and redirect it.
verdicts.rationale: The skeptical position cites a quantified failure of the most-resourced existing booked-value auditor (the IRS losing roughly $160 billion annually to transfer-pricing and IP-migration), demonstrating that the auditing capability the proposed body requires is unproven at scale. The defense of an independent body relies on an analogy to aircraft accident investigators and the Boeing-FAA reporting-line fix, which establishes that structural separation can address capture but does not establish that booked-value auditing of mobile AI surplus is operationally achievable. The two failure modes are distinct (capture versus enforcement capacity), and the proposed architecture answers only the first.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: A working deployment of a tax or audit body that recovers a measurable share of booked digital or IP surplus despite transfer-pricing avoidance would support the viability of the proposed architecture.

verdicts.conflict: What 'worker ownership' must mean to capture surplus—tool access, an audited transfer on the worker's behalf, or a contractual bargaining mechanism with power to refuse.
verdicts.rationale: This is a definitional dispute (bdi_layer intention) rather than an empirical one, so the preference criteria adjudicate term clarity rather than truth. The bargaining-mechanism definition is the most concrete and testable, supplying a falsifiable marker (documented refusal-power that changed a firm's deployment, per C25), but the access and audit definitions each specify enforceable mechanisms (a non-relocatable weights file; a named actor auditing booked value). Because each position names a distinct institutional claim and the disagreement turns on a value choice about what counts as ownership, no single definition dominates on evidence.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Agreement on a shared success metric—such as recovered wage share, an enforceable contractual claim on surplus, or demonstrated refusal-power—would convert this definitional dispute into a resolvable empirical comparison.

verdicts.conflict: Whether current AI adoption in clerical and support work is regenerative dynamism creating new roles or pure labor-arbitrage substitution.
verdicts.rationale: The substitution position cites a specific present-day price mechanism (a $25/hour task replaced by a $2 inference call) and the Copilot evidence of flat wages alongside higher output, and the opposing claimant explicitly concedes that most current adoption is cost-cutting arbitrage (C15). The dynamism position relies on a historical analogy (bank teller headcount growing through 2010 after ATMs, per Bessen) whose applicability to cognitive-task automation is contested by the price-substitution evidence. The concession in C15 narrows the live disagreement to a forward-looking claim about net demand not reaching zero, which is supported by absence of contrary evidence rather than by positive evidence.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Longitudinal data showing net new cognitive-labor roles and recovering wages in sectors where AI has already been deployed at scale would support the dynamism reading over the substitution reading.
